areaFindings.name: Crate/module decomposition and the host / pure-core boundary
areaFindings.whatIWouldBuild: Workspace exactly as IMPLEMENTER-BLUEPRINT.md §4: bins/opensip, crates/{host,core,types,plan,facts,rules,policy,evidence,store,provider-protocol,facts-ts,facts-rust,versioning,delivery}, bins/{typescript-provider,rust-provider}. Dependency direction from the §4 tree. The five forbidden-edge classes become cargo-deny / a compile-time workspace test in commit 1.
whyItIsEnough: Each package has an explicit Owns column AND an explicit 'Must not own or import' column — the second column is what actually prevents drift.

R-1 §rustApi fixes the boundary in one line: evaluate(stageInput: &SealedStageInput, deps: &CoreDeps, attempt: &AttemptMetadata) -> CoreCompletion, with a closed forbiddenPublicShapes list (no dyn Trait, no Fn argument, no &mut input, no CoreCompletion<'a>, no async, no evaluate_resident, no evaluate_with_ports).

CoreDeps carries an explicit forbiddenFields list of 20 names (resourceMeter, diagnostics, clock, entropy, filesystem, network, traitObject, ...). There is no space for an implementer to 'just inject a port'.
The blueprint states plainly that the proposed `store` crate is an implementation of the single durable-state authority, not a peer authority.
residualsHit: crates/evidence and crates/store can be laid out as empty boundaries only — their value schemas are Phase-1A/EVIDENCE-blocked (named).

areaFindings.couldStartMonday: YES for the core and plan planes; NO for the evidence plane
areaFindings.whatIWouldBuild: Day one: R-1 closedTypes verbatim — Digest, OpaqueId, U64, U128, ExecutionId, CanonicalValueRef, SealedStageInput, AttemptMetadata, RuleValue, RuleSet, PolicyValue, BudgetLimits, CoreDeps, FindingValue, FindingList, CoverageState, CoverageEntry, ExactCoverage, PolicyOutcome, DiagnosticRecord, DiagnosticsData, BudgetUsage, FactDeficiency, D9NormalizedFaultCause, CoreCompletion. Then C-2 PlanIntent/AdmissionDescriptorV1/StoredViewIntentV1/ExecutionPlan/coverageKey, RESOLVED-INPUTS PlanDescriptorV1 and the two semanticUniverse schemas, D9 HostTermination union.

Blueprint §5 carries an honest preamble saying the 'First API / type' column is PROPOSED Rust naming and that where it disagrees with the artifact, the artifact wins. It even names the specific disagreements (FACT-IDENTITY spells them normalisationLadder/anchorValidation/budgetModel; FACT-PLANE has no CoverageEntry). This is exactly the disclosure an implementer needs and it is unusual to find it.

areaFindings.name: Fact provider interface AND the Rust sidecar wire protocol (framing, message types, FSM, cancel/unavailable)
areaFindings.couldStartMonday: YES for the byte protocol and FSM; PARTIAL for the fate-normalization and Plan-projection halves; NO for Coverage-key construction
areaFindings.confidence: high on the protocol, low on reachability of the joins

whatIsFullyThere.framing: 8-byte big-endian payloadLength, then 32 raw SHA-256 digest bytes, then payloadLength canonical-CBOR bytes. prefixBytes 40. lengthScope payload-only. Reject over-length BEFORE allocation. stdout is protocol-only from child start to EOF; EOF is valid only in WAIT_EOF after one valid worker terminal and observed zero exit.
whatIsFullyThere.canonicalCbor: RFC 8949 core deterministic, an 8-member closed data model, an 11-member explicit forbidden list, and an exact map-ordering rule (by encoded-key byte length, then lexicographic). decodeRule requires decode-then-re-encode byte equality.
whatIsFullyThere.messageTypes: 21 frame types with direction and workerTerminal flags: Hello/HelloAck, OpenUniverse/UniverseAccepted, SnapshotManifest/SnapshotFileChunk/SnapshotSeal/SnapshotAccepted, PreparedOutputManifest/Chunk/Seal/Accepted, Analyze, FactBatch, Coverage, and the five worker-terminal frames Unavailable, BudgetExhausted, Complete, ProviderFault, Cancelled, plus host Cancel. Every payload has a closed schema.
whatIsFullyThere.fsm: orderingAndStateMachineV4 is a closed typed deterministic transition transaction: 13 phases, an explicit initialState record, 28 priority-ordered transition rules with guards and actions, a fallbackRule, closed precheck/transition result unions, phaseEventCompatibility, and a semanticConformanceVectors set.
whatIsFullyThere.cancelAndUnavailable: cancelPermittedPhases lists all 13 phases; providerFaultPermittedPhases lists 12 (START excluded). Unavailable and BudgetExhausted are worker-terminal frames, and DELIVERY terminationIntegration + freeze §3.2 item 4 make them exact Coverage rather than faults.
whatIsFullyThere.limits: 24 numeric limits including cancellationGraceMilliseconds 5000 and normalExitGraceMilliseconds 5000, plus a limitsHandshake requiring byte equality with the top-level limits.
whatIsFullyThere.hostFinalizerBoundary: delivery-rust-provider-join.v4#hostFinalizerBoundaryV4 is present inline, carries the exact pinned scenarioAxesSchema, and states the rule that the host recomputes the D9 axes and never accepts a provider-produced class, code or axis.

areaFindings.whatIsNotReachableFrom11: The 16-row priority-ordered fate reducer (orderedNormalizationReducerV2: USER_INTERRUPTED > DELIVERY_REQUIRED_FAILURE > POST_TERMINAL_OUTPUT > MALFORMED_FRAME > SCHEMA_OR_COMMITMENT_FAULT > HANDSHAKE_MISMATCH > DEADLINE_HANG > NONZERO_EXIT > EARLY_EOF > UNSOLICITED_CANCELLED > PROVIDER_DECLARED_FAULT > VERIFIED_COMPLETE > VERIFIED_UNAVAILABLE > VERIFIED_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED > VERIFIED_CANCELLED > INCOMPLETE_PROTOCOL) together with providerObservationV2, compositeObservationV2, normalizedFateCustody, launch, processModel and diagnosticsAndScratchBounds exists ONLY in delivery-rust-provider-join.v2.json. I verified by key comparison that none of those seven selectors is present in the pinned v4 file. The same is true of resolved-inputs-rust-provider-join.v4, whose entire semantic content is a projection of thirteen selectors in the unpinned v2. See ESC2-F02.

factProviderInterface.finding: There is deliberately NO common FactProvider trait, and the blueprint says so: crates/provider-protocol must not own 'a single merged one-protocol abstraction that erases the two transports' differences'. That is a decision made FOR the implementer and it is the right kind of instruction.
factProviderInterface.hostSideDomainConstruction: rust-provider-protocol.v2#planAndDomainProjection gives exact algorithms for sourceUniverseId, allSemanticUniverseIdAlgorithm, subjectsAlgorithm (with the subject-ID domain separator opensip.rust-provider.subject.v2) and coverageDomainAlgorithm with a canonical relation/rung/target nested-loop order. This is implementable as written.
factProviderInterface.blocker: coverageDomainAlgorithm emits a C-2 Coverage key containing subjectScopeCommitment, which no artifact defines. So the domain construction is fully specified except for one field, and without that field no Coverage key can be constructed at all. This is on the ANALYSIS path, not merely the evidence path — a point freeze §7.1 understates.

areaFindings.typescriptSide: DELIVERY typescriptSemanticSubstrate carries a complete frameEnvelope, HelloV1/HelloAckV1 handshake with the full identity set, one child per (ExecutionId, SnapshotId, TypeScriptSemanticUniverseKey), no reuse or multiplexing, absolute-path spawn of the signed bundled runtime with no PATH/NODE_PATH/NODE_OPTIONS consultation, and sealed-VFS-only reads. I could build this. It has no numeric supervision timeouts (the Rust side does).

areaFindings.name: Evidence — what must be persisted for an authoritative Run, in what shape
areaFindings.confidence: certain, and the package is certain too
areaFindings.finding: The package does not merely leave this under-specified; it explicitly prohibits building it. §1.1 note N-3: 'No EVIDENCE bytes are normative right now. Do not port bundle-shape fixtures, and do not implement universeCommitment, outcomeSetDigest, SubjectSetCommitment, EvidenceDigest or any bundle identity from any current version.' Blueprint §5 repeats it, §7.2 step 6 formally WITHDRAWS the previous instruction to port bundle fixtures, and freeze §3 marks EVIDENCE 'UNSET — BLOCKS FREEZE'.
areaFindings.assessment: This is the correct behavior for a package with a rejected head. An implementer is not left guessing; they are told to stop. That is a pass on packaging and a fail on architecture completeness, and the package says exactly that. I would lay out the crates/evidence boundary and write nothing inside it.

areaFindings.name: Retention/custody — what the host must do before the first durable write, and what happens when evidence is later unavailable
areaFindings.couldStartMonday: YES for the pre-first-write half; NO for the retention/degradation half

sequence: Canonicalise and open the admitted storage root; retain the root handle for root-confined operations.
Validate storage-root.v1.json — exactly {schemaVersion, rootId}, rootId matching ^root1-[0-9a-f]{32}$, allocated as 16 CSPRNG bytes with create-new + fsync, never derived from path or ProjectId.

Run the signed detector catalog (sync-provider-declared-root, ci-upload-workspace-policy, os-backup-membership, effective-permissions) and apply the admission decision table: cloud-sync-or-ci-upload/DETECTED = REFUSE, permission-exposed/DETECTED = REFUSE, backup-managed/DETECTED = REQUIRE-EXPLICIT-POLICY-AND-DISCLOSE, any/UNKNOWN = DO-NOT-CLAIM-SAFE.
Verify filesystem support (WAL, atomic link) and refuse unsupported/networked roots rather than assuming.

Resolve exactly one physical projects/<ProjectId> namespace from a host-verified typed ProjectId used byte-for-byte as one path component, rejecting uppercase, separators, dot segments, percent escapes, lookalikes and normalization-on-read. No cross-project physical dedup.
Admit the AttemptRecord transactionally before snapshot work.

For publication: write, checksum, fsync and atomically link CAS objects first, then publish refs and the sealed Run in one idempotent ledger transaction. Recovery may collect an unreferenced object; it may never infer a sealed success from one.
preFirstDurableWriteIsBuildable.verdict: This is genuinely enough to write the storage-admission module and its negative controls.

areaFindings.name: Termination — can exit class and code be derived for a given scenario purely from the contracts?
areaFindings.couldStartMonday: YES for every cause-bearing scenario; NO for the causeless branch; and the named oracle is not where the package says it is
whatIsDerivable: exitClasses and classToExitCode are total and explicit: success 0, policy-failed 1, request-rejected 2, indeterminate 3, operational-failed 4, interrupted 130.

crossAxisInvariants X1/X2/X3 are biconditional: deficiency != none <-> indeterminate; rejectionCause != none <-> request-rejected; faultCause != none <-> operational-failed. X4 forbids more than one non-none family. So for any scenario with a cause, the class is DETERMINED by the axes with no further rule needed.

codeMaps are declared total and injective over all three families, and codeDerivation states the full ordered list rule: indeterminate emits [map(deficiency)] + [map(d) for d in secondaryDeficiencies]; request-rejected and operational-failed emit one errorCode; success/policy-failed/interrupted emit no code field.
causeModel.precedence (faultCause > rejectionCause > deficiency) plus concurrentConditionReducer resolves genuinely concurrent conditions.
hostTerminationUnion gives per-variant required/optional fields, forbids exitCode on the payload entirely, and states nullabilityPolicy (absent, never explicit null).
whatIsNotDerivable: Observation-to-faultCause selection: which physical failure maps to host-io vs cas-link vs durability-commit. Named as a contract gap in freeze §3 D9 row.
Optional-field presence policy: when runId/executionId/coverageId must actually be populated. Named in the same row.

The success / policy-failed / interrupted branch when all three cause families are none — in particular the precedence between interruption=signal-before-finalization and verdict=fail. Named in the same row.
request-rejected `details` is typed only as {type: object} with no schema, while DELIVERY requires it to carry FEATURE.REQUIRES_CAPABILITY_RUNTIME or FEATURE.EXTERNAL_SCANNER_NOT_IN_V1. Not named.
areaFindings.workedExample: Scenario: the required Rust semantic universe cannot be constructed. Axes: commandKind=run, admission=admitted, lifecycle=coherent-terminal-run, requiredCoverage=unsatisfied, verdict=indeterminate, durability=committed, interruption=none, requiredPostconditions=met, domainCondition=none, deficiency=provider-unavailable, rejectionCause=none, faultCause=none, secondaryDeficiencies=[]. By X1, class=indeterminate. By codeDerivation, reasonCodes=[COVERAGE.PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE]. By classToExitCode, exit 3. Union variant indeterminate requires reasonCodes and permits runId/coverageId/executionId. I derived this end to end from the JSON with no checker. This is the v1-slice §7.7 fixture and it works.
areaFindings.unnamedProblemFound: The named derivation oracle does not contain the derivation. See ESC2-B01.

escalations.title: The D9 axes-to-class derivation is not in any byte pinned by §1.1, and the only route to it runs through an independently REJECTED contract version that the package's own version rule forbids building
escalations.whatINeeded: The pure function from scenarioAxes to HostTermination class, for the branch the JSON does not state (success / policy-failed / interrupted, and the interruption-vs-verdict precedence). Blueprint §7.2 step 1 makes this the FIRST thing to port.
whereILooked: d9-exit-contract.v1.13.json — states exitClasses, classToExitCode, codeMaps, X1-X11, 45 goldens, but no class-selection function for the causeless branch. Its referenceDerivation field names 'artifacts/check-d9-v1.13.py::check+derive_class+derive_codes+reduce_concurrent+V17.V16.derive_class'.
IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §2, which puts check-d9-v1.13.py in the signed payload and declares it 'normative for the axes-to-class step the D9 JSON does not itself state'.
IMPLEMENTER-BLUEPRINT.md §5 D9 row, which calls it 'the pure derivation oracle' and 'the port target'.
escalations.whyInsufficient: check-d9-v1.13.py contains no derivation. Its derive_class is a one-line delegation to check-d9-v1.12.py, which delegates to check-d9-v1.11.py, which delegates to check-d9-v1.10.py, where the body first appears (line 769). Reaching it requires loading 22 pinned files, of which exactly one (d9-exit-contract.v1.13.json) appears in §1.1. Two of the required contracts — d9-exit-contract.v1.12.json and, through it, the whole v1.11/v1.10/v1.9/v1.8/v1.7/v1.6 lineage — are superseded, and the v1.13 checker positively ASSERTS that the pinned v1.12 review is 'the exact REJECT' with blockingFindingCount 1. The closure also pins retention-tiers.v14.json and check-retention-custody-v14.py, i.e. a superseded V10/retention candidate, while note N-4 tells the implementer not to implement retention from candidates. Blueprint §1.1 rule 3 says a REJECTED version 'is not implementable' and rule 4 says a superseded version 'is not a fallback ... Do not build a lower version'. The instructions and the artifact structure are in direct opposition.
escalations.couldAnEngineerGuessWrong: Yes, three different ways, all defensible: (a) read check-d9-v1.10.py and port its body, knowingly violating the stated version rule; (b) treat the chain as untrustworthy because it is rooted on a REJECTED contract and write their own axes-to-class function from the 45 goldens, which under-constrains the causeless branch; (c) stall. (a) and (b) diverge on exactly the interruption-vs-verdict precedence that is the open question. The v1.10 body checks interruption BEFORE verdict, so a signal-before-finalization on a failing policy run yields interrupted (130) rather than policy-failed (1). An engineer deriving from the exitClasses prose alone can easily reach the opposite. Different exit codes for the same run is a week-one fork with CI consequences.
escalations.whatWouldCloseIt: Either state the axes-to-class function in d9-exit-contract at the head, or extend §1.1 to pin the full D9 authority closure with an explicit carve-out from rule 4 explaining why executing a REJECTED predecessor's checker is legitimate here.

escalations.title: The §1.1 pin table is not transitively closed: the two Rust join artifacts are projection shells whose load-bearing content lives in unpinned predecessors
escalations.whatINeeded: The provider fate-normalization reducer, the provider/composite observation records, launch and process-model rules, and the Plan/ToolPath projection — i.e. the cancel/unavailable/fault path the milestone golden 'Rust provider crash/truncated frame' depends on.
whereILooked: delivery-rust-provider-join.v4.json (pinned) — contains hostFinalizerBoundaryV4 and reducerPreservation, but its retainedV2SemanticProjection inherits processModel, ownership, launch, diagnosticsAndScratchBounds, d9Reference, providerObservationV2, compositeObservationV2, orderedNormalizationReducerV2 and normalizedFateCustody BY REFERENCE from delivery-rust-provider-join.v2.json, which is not pinned in §1.1.

resolved-inputs-rust-provider-join.v4.json (pinned) — its ENTIRE semantic content is exactSemanticProjectionOfV2 over thirteen selectors of resolved-inputs-rust-provider-join.v2.json, plus retainedV3ExactProjection over .v3.json. Neither is pinned.

rust-provider-protocol.v4.json — retainedV3RepairBoundary requires hashing six further files including rust-provider-protocol.v3.json, which v4's own predecessorRejection records as REJECT with three blocking findings.
escalations.whyInsufficient: I verified by direct key comparison that seven load-bearing selectors present in the v2 join are absent from the v4 join. §1.1 note N-2 shows the authors understood this pattern exactly — it pins BOTH rust-provider-protocol.v2 and .v4 and says 'Both digests are pinned above because you need both files' — but the same treatment was not applied to the two join artifacts or to the v3 repair boundaries. Measured: the 22 pinned artifacts reference 55 further files with inline digests that are not in §1.1. All 55 exist and all 55 digests match live bytes, so this is a packaging omission, not corruption.
escalations.couldAnEngineerGuessWrong: Yes. One engineer follows the artifact's own projection rule, opens the v2 files, and implements the 16-row priority reducer correctly. Another obeys blueprint §1.1 rule 4 literally, refuses to build a superseded version, and either invents a fate ordering or leaves the supervisor's failure classification undefined. The reducer's ordering is not obvious — for example USER_INTERRUPTED outranks DELIVERY_REQUIRED_FAILURE, and UNSOLICITED_CANCELLED (terminalKind=cancelled with hostCancelSent=false) is a distinct fate from VERIFIED_CANCELLED. Getting that wrong changes the D9 class for a whole family of provider failures.
escalations.whatWouldCloseIt: Add the four join predecessors, rust-provider-protocol.v3, and the D9 closure to §1.1 with a stated 'inheritance base, not a fallback' role, exactly as N-2 already does for rust-provider-protocol.v2.

escalations.title: protocolMajor for the Rust sidecar is 1 in RESOLVED-INPUTS and DELIVERY and 2 in RUST-PROVIDER-PROTOCOL, and the disagreement changes the PlanId
escalations.whatINeeded: The single integer to put in the rust-semantic semanticUniverse key (PLAN-ID-V1 preimage tag 9) and on the wire in HelloAckV2.
whereILooked: resolved-inputs.v2.json#planIdContract.semanticUniverseSchemas.rust-v1 requires protocolMajor, and its deliveryJoin states verbatim that 'protocolMajor, providerBuildId, rustCommitHash, hostTriple, targetTriple and sysrootDigest equal the validated bundled rustc_driver sidecar handshake'.
resolved-inputs.v2.json golden vector planid-v1-ci-full-providers, whose rust universe carries protocolMajor: 1.
resolved-inputs-rust-provider-join.v4.json and delivery-rust-provider-join.v4.json — neither mentions protocolMajor at all.
escalations.whyInsufficient: Blueprint §3.3 resolves DELIVERY-vs-RPP in RPP's favour, so the handshake value is 2. RESOLVED-INPUTS then says the universe-key field EQUALS the handshake, which forces 2. But the frozen, independently PASSED PlanId golden bakes in 1. RESOLVED-INPUTS is not DELIVERY, so §3.3's tie-break does not reach it, and no document states a tie-break for RESOLVED-INPUTS vs RUST-PROVIDER-PROTOCOL.
escalations.measuredConsequence: I recomputed the golden with protocolMajor flipped from 1 to 2. Expected/golden PlanId: plan1:sha256:86ccc0baa679dec956c0ca310889798e6b45ebbc7e11157f71e636dbf2f68401. With the handshake value: plan1:sha256:c577afd32665f75e53abc60a6423fefd55bc11431d70996fee75762ae852b233. Two defensible readings, two different PlanIds.
escalations.couldAnEngineerGuessWrong: Yes, and the two engineers most likely to disagree are the one porting the RESOLVED-INPUTS goldens (gets 1) and the one implementing the sidecar handshake (gets 2). v1-slice §7.1 makes 'emits a deterministic PlanId' the first milestone-exit observation, so the fork lands directly on the exit criterion. It also lands on the RPP frame envelope, since a host sending protocolMajor 1 to a sidecar requiring exactly 2 is an immediate handshake mismatch.
escalations.complianceNote: IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §8 permits escalating 'a detected conflict with a binding artifact', so raising this is technically compliant. I still count it as an unnamed FORK because the package presents both artifacts as independently PASSED at these exact digests and nothing warns that they disagree. This conflict was invisible to the first litmus precisely because RUST-PROVIDER-PROTOCOL was then unreachable — repairing that defect exposed this one.

escalations.title: FACT-PLANE confidence is a load-bearing number that no contract says how to compute
escalations.whatINeeded: How a producer computes FactEnvelope entry.confidence, since a requirement's minConfidence floor and the confidence-floor-unmet deficiency both depend on it.
whereILooked: fact-plane.v1.json#sufficiency.rule (satisfied requires 'confidence >= minConfidence'), #deficiencyDiscrimination.cases (confidence-floor-unmet is a distinct remedy class added by R1-FP-01 adjudication), #requirementSchema.minConfidence (default 0.0), #factEnvelope.
fact-identity-policy.v2.json, delivery.v2.json, rust-provider-protocol.v2.json — no confidence computation rule.
escalations.whyInsufficient: fact-plane.v1#knownLimitations[1] states it outright: 'Confidence is typed as a number in [0,1] but this contract does not say how any producer computes one. A floor over an uncomputed number is not yet meaningful.' That admission is inside a binding artifact but appears in NO residual table in the package. IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §8 restricts compliant escalation to the §7 table, the §7.1 recipes and the two named gaps under it, the PHASE-1A markers, and digest mismatches. An artifact-internal knownLimitation is none of those.
escalations.couldAnEngineerGuessWrong: Yes. One producer returns 1.0 for everything (making the floor inert and confidence-floor-unmet unreachable), another returns a heuristic score. That flips the reported deficiency between confidence-floor-unmet and required-relation-missing, which per fact-plane's own remedy taxonomy tells the user to do two different things, and both map to different D9 reasonCodes.
escalations.mitigation: Defaulting minConfidence to 0.0 makes the floor inert by default, so this is not immediately fatal for the toy-fixture milestone. Severity is FORK rather than BLOCKING for that reason.

escalations.title: OPERABILITY G19 says the initial product rejects durable-authoritative retention; v1-slice makes an authoritative sealed Run the milestone exit
escalations.whatINeeded: Whether to build the authoritative durable path at all in the v1 slice, or ship ephemeral/advisory-only until Phase 1A lands.
whereILooked: operability.v10.json#validationGates G19: status BLOCKED-NO-MECHANISM, blocker TM.V10 / ARCH.RETENTION-TIERS, and initialProductDisposition verbatim: 'durable-authoritative retention is rejected; only explicit ephemeral/advisory operation is available until the proof/custody decision is selected'.

v1-slice.md §2.5 ('Persist the minimum authoritative evidence needed to validate and inspect a sealed Run from a second process') and §7 steps 4-5 (persist the proof, seal the Run, second process reads and validates it).
IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §4.1, which lists 'the Phase-1A authoritative evidence path, Run seal, D9 termination, and second-process inspect' as required.
escalations.whyInsufficient: Both defer to Phase 1A, but they point opposite directions in the meantime. OPERABILITY states a positive interim product behavior (ephemeral/advisory only) that no package document repeats or contradicts. The freeze frames the V10 hole as 'insert the decision later', which reads as 'build the path, fill in the policy'. G19 reads as 'do not build the authoritative path yet'.
escalations.couldAnEngineerGuessWrong: Yes — this determines whether crates/store ships a Run-sealing path in the first milestone or an explicitly-ephemeral mode. That is a large structural difference in the store crate and in the CLI's default behavior.
escalations.marginalImpact: Low in practice, because everything downstream is already V10-blocked and blueprint §9 forbids starting product code before a signed freeze. Recorded because a blind implementer reading the binding artifact does hit it and no document names it.

escalations.title: fact-plane.v1 hard-references d9-exit-contract.v1.6.json, a version the blueprint explicitly disowns
escalations.detail: fact-plane.v1.json#deficiencyVocabulary.mustBeSubsetOf points at 'd9-exit-contract.v1.6.json#scenarioAxesSchema.properties.deficiency.enum', and its stated purpose is that F9 checks the live D9 artifact 'rather than restating it, so the two cannot drift'. Blueprint §1.1 names v1.6 among five stale links and notes it self-declares CANDIDATE-UNREVIEWED. So the anti-drift mechanism is anchored to a version the package forbids. Resolvable by §1.1 rule 1 (it is a pointer, not authority) and the two enums do intersect correctly, so no implementer action is blocked. The retained check-fact-plane.py will still read v1.6.

escalations.title: The rust-provider-protocol v2/v4 merge algorithm is not fully mechanical for three keys
escalations.detail: mergeAlgorithm says 'overlay the named v4 sections. Any absent, extra, reordered array, changed scalar/type, or unlisted overlay rejects v4.' But v4 carries six top-level sections that are in neither inheritedTopLevelSelectors nor replacedSelectors: schemaLanguageV4, closureClaims, predecessorRejection, retainedV3RepairBoundary, retainedV2SemanticProjection, and dependencyPins. dependencyPins is worse than merely unlisted: it appears in inheritedTopLevelSelectors (retain the v2 value, 6 entries) AND in v4 with 18 entries, with no precedence rule. schemaLanguage is retained from v2 while schemaLanguageV4 is overlaid, so the merged object carries both. In practice they address different domains (v2's is the wire schema language, v4's is the FSM AST language) and dependencyPins is provenance, so nothing load-bearing forks. Recorded because a strict implementation of the stated rule rejects v4.

escalations.title: IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §7.1 misstates the Finding gap
escalations.detail: The Finding-fingerprint row asserts 'No artifact defines a Finding schema.' r1-lifetime-neutrality.conformance.v1.5.json#closedTypes.FindingValue does define one: a closed record {ruleId: OpaqueId, findingId: OpaqueId, valueDigest: Digest} with explicit fieldOrder and additionalProperties:false, plus FindingList. The real gap — that findingId and valueDigest have no derivation recipe — is genuine and the escalation instruction is right. Only the justification is inaccurate. An implementer who takes the sentence literally may spend time inventing a Finding type that already exists.

escalations.title: operability.v10 carries exitCode inside a d9Termination object that D9 forbids

sufficiencyList.purpose: Recorded with equal weight to the escalations. Over-correcting a package that is already strong in these places would be a worse outcome than the remaining gaps.

items.finding: All 22 §1.1 digests recompute exactly against live bytes, and no package document links a binding artifact at a non-head version. I verified both mechanically. The four reading rules (digest is the contract; self-declared status is not a verdict; PASSED means one independent reviewer with zero blockers and nothing more; a superseded version is not a fallback) are the right four rules and are stated crisply.

PLAN-ID-V1 and CVE1 are byte-exactly reproducible from prose alone. I implemented both cold and hit the expected preimage byte lengths (2500, 8208) and both golden digests on the first attempt. This is a genuinely high standard and the package is right to hold successors to it.
planIntentCommitment and opensip-canonical-json-v1 are equally reproducible: seven of seven valid C-2 fixtures on the first attempt. The tag-13 join between C-2 and RESOLVED-INPUTS is exact.

R-1 fixes the pure core with one signature, 25 closed types with field order and bounds, a 9-item forbiddenPublicShapes list, and a 20-name CoreDeps forbiddenFields list. There is no room for an implementer to negotiate a port into the core.

The §4 workspace map's second column ('must not own or import') plus the five forbidden dependency-edge classes turn architecture into a test that runs from commit one. The explicit instruction that crates/store is an implementation of the durable authority rather than a peer authority pre-empts the most likely drift.

Framing, deterministic-CBOR profile with an explicit forbidden list and exact map ordering, 21 typed frames with direction and terminality, a 28-rule priority FSM with an explicit initial state, cancelPermittedPhases, providerFaultPermittedPhases, 24 numeric limits with a handshake equality requirement, and a conformance corpus. Two engineers can build interoperable implementations from this. It is the strongest single artifact in the package.

For any scenario carrying a cause, class and code are fully determined by the axes: X1/X2/X3 are biconditional, X4 enforces exclusivity, codeMaps are total and injective, and codeDerivation states the ordered list rule. I derived the provider-unavailable exit path end to end from the JSON with no checker.

TRUSTED-REQUEST-CONTEXT gives enough to write the type on Monday: opaque, no public constructors, non-copyable, non-serializable, minted only by a TrustedHostRequestAuthorityV3 trusted-ingress operation, with the selected authority instance — not the context, not a module global — owning the exactly-once reservation registry, and an explicit prohibition on ambient singletons, thread locals, Clone and serializable tokens. 5 positive plus 30 adversarial controls.

The pre-first-durable-write obligation is fully buildable: root canonicalization and open, storage-root.v1.json with an exact rootId pattern and 16-byte CSPRNG create-new+fsync allocation, a signed detector catalog with a four-row admission decision table including an explicit 'UNKNOWN means do not claim safe', ProjectId used byte-for-byte as one path component with a closed rejection list, a ban on cross-project physical dedup, and journaled purge/migration state machines rather than recursive delete.

The lifecycle order is unambiguous and repeated identically in the mermaid flow, the nine numbered consequences, and the §6 pseudocode: RequestId minted and reserved before parsing; PlanIntent validated, frozen and committed before ExecutionId exists; stored-view creating no attempt, no Plan, no Run; substitution after admission rejected before any stage. C-2's insistence that resolution precedes attempt admission — and the explicit warning not to implement 'admit then PlanId' literally — pre-empts the obvious wrong reading.

Every product disposition an implementer could otherwise invent is decided: CI never loads or resolves layer 4, pivot only on explicit comparison plus detector major with INDETERMINATE when unavailable, P-1 no depth, P-2 narrow, no public rule-IR freeze, support windows visibly provisional. The blueprint states these as removals of implementation choice, which is the right framing.

C-1 is made mechanical rather than aspirational: 12 relations with explicit weakest-first ladders, single-rung relations declared non-degradable (the `declares` note is the canonical case), a closed 5-value deficiency vocabulary ordered by remedy specificity, a completenessRule forbidding unknown coverage from satisfying `complete`, and an authoritativeRule forbidding a deficiency on a satisfied top-rung requirement. No global tier ordering is expressible.

The package repeatedly refuses to overclaim in ways that materially helped me: §7.2 step 6 formally withdraws a previous instruction; §6.6 formally withdraws a previous false assertion about RunId; §1.1 rule 2 warns that an artifact's self-declared status is not a review verdict; §8.3 separates IMPLEMENTABLE / QUALIFIED / DEMONSTRATED; §7.1 states plainly that naming a gap does not close it. Withdrawn instructions are marked as withdrawn rather than silently deleted, which is what let me trust the rest.

Freeze §8 defines the named escalation set precisely enough to be testable, and §9.1 adds mechanical verification checkboxes including digest equality between §3 and §1.1 and a prohibition on linking any non-head version. That is why this run could produce a countable verdict rather than an impression.

verdict.criterion: ARCHITECTURE-TO-IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN.md §1.3 / G5 and IMPLEMENTATION-FREEZE.md §8: an implementer may escalate only a named residual or a detected conflict with a binding artifact. Escalating anything unnamed is a failure.

counts.carryoverNote: ESC-25 from litmus v1 is verified still live and still unnamed. I did not raise it independently, but a conscientious implementer would, so the honest unnamed BLOCKING+FORK figure is 6.

comparisonToLitmusV1.reduction: 75% reduction in unnamed BLOCKING+FORK escalations. All three of litmus v1's named clusters were addressed: the version-selection cluster is fixed and mechanically verifiable, the orphaned Rust protocol is fully reachable and byte-complete, and the six parked identity recipes are named accurately enough that escalating them is now compliant.

verdict.statement: The repair worked on its own terms and did not work completely. Litmus v1's three diagnosed defects are genuinely addressed, and I could verify two of them mechanically rather than by reading assurances: 22 of 22 pinned digests match, no package document links a non-head version, the Rust wire protocol merges cleanly and specifies framing, frames, FSM, cancel and unavailable at the byte level, and PLAN-ID-V1 plus planIntentCommitment reproduced byte-exactly on the first attempt. The residual failure has a single dominant root cause and it is a NEW one created by the repair itself: introducing a pin table made transitive closure a meaningful question for the first time, and the table is not closed. The D9 axes-to-class oracle the package names is an empty delegation shell whose real body sits three checker generations back behind an independently REJECTED contract, and the two Rust join artifacts are projection shells over unpinned predecessors that hold the entire provider fate-normalization reducer. A second, independent new finding — protocolMajor 1 versus 2 producing two different PlanIds for the same universe — was likewise only discoverable because the Rust protocol became reachable. That is the healthy shape of a second litmus: the previous round's fixes are real, and they surfaced the next layer.
whatWouldMakeItPass: Extend §1.1 to the transitive closure, with an explicit role label distinguishing 'inheritance base you must read' from 'superseded, do not build' — the treatment note N-2 already gives rust-provider-protocol.v2, applied to delivery-rust-provider-join.v2/v3, resolved-inputs-rust-provider-join.v2/v3, rust-provider-protocol.v3, and the D9 checker/contract chain including retention-tiers.v14.
Either state the D9 axes-to-class function in the head contract, or point referenceDerivation at the file that actually contains it and justify executing a REJECTED predecessor's checker.
Adjudicate protocolMajor for the Rust semantic universe and reissue the affected PlanId golden, or state the tie-break between RESOLVED-INPUTS and RUST-PROVIDER-PROTOCOL.
Name FACT-PLANE confidence, the OPERABILITY G19 interim disposition, the D9 `details` schema, and the TypeScript supervision numerics in a residual table, or close them.
Fix the concurrentConditionGoldens 'invalid-config' spelling at the D9 head.
verdict.notADeclaration: This record declares no seal, no freeze, no product acceptance, and no disposition of any surface. It closes no finding and unblocks no gate. It is one blind implementer's readiness assessment of a package that is explicitly marked NOT FROZEN and that forbids starting product code before signature.

establishes: That an implementer reading only the four package documents and what they point to can, or cannot, reach a specific normative value without guessing. That is a reachability property of the delivered package and it is what this run measured.

That specific recipes are reproducible from prose alone: I re-derived PLAN-ID-V1, CVE1 and planIntentCommitment cold, first attempt, matching exact preimage byte lengths and digests. A reproduction claim backed by executed code is stronger than a reading.

That specific pointers are broken: the D9 referenceDerivation target contains no derivation, and two pinned join artifacts contain none of the semantics they are cited for. Both are demonstrable by inspection and neither depends on my judgement.
That two independently PASSED artifacts disagree on a value that changes a frozen golden PlanId. I computed both resulting digests.
doesNotEstablish: That the architecture is correct. I assessed whether it is buildable as written, not whether building it is a good idea.

That the surfaces I could implement are semantically right. Reproducing a golden proves I matched the author's arithmetic, not that the identity model is sound. The D9 artifact makes this point about its own goldens and it applies to my reproductions too.
